result:
**Ordering: Extract by dependency direction, not by feature.**

Start with stateless services that don't depend on other new services (bottom of the dependency graph). Pull out payment processing before auth, auth before user-facing features. This prevents cascading rewrites. Second: isolate high-changefreq or resource-contended components early (search, caching, slow background jobs). Third: tackle human-heavy domains (reporting, admin tools) last; they tolerate slower rollout.

**Data ownership: Strangle the DB, not the code.**

Don't rewrite the service code first. Instead, add a new service + new DB table. Write an **anti-corruption layer** in the monolith that syncs between old and new schemas (event log, polling, or dual-write). For months, both exist; the new service owns its table, but the monolith still owns the source. When the new service stabilizes, flip the switch: monolith calls the service, new DB becomes canonical. Only delete the old table after 2–3 deploys clean (catches rollback bugs). This decouples service readiness from schema migration.

**Keeping it shippable: One extracted service per sprint, always runnable.**

Extract one service fully per cycle—from code split to production, tested with real traffic. Use **feature flags** or router rules to shard traffic to the new service (1% → 10% → 100%), not to revert mid-deploy. Each extraction is a PR; each PR lands in main and ships. The monolith shrinks with each deploy. Parallel extraction of unrelated services halves risk (e.g., search and auth don't touch each other, so extract both at once). Keep an **integration test suite** that runs monolith + all live services to catch data path breaks early.

**The real gotcha:** Distributed transactions. When the monolith and new service must coordinate (e.g., "debit wallet, then order"), use sagas (choreography via events) or orchestration (monolith coordinates). This is where incremental extraction gets messy; plan it early, use the anti-corruption layer to log events that services can consume.
